chapters.name: Chapter 1: Know your record and your options

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting a copy of your own record
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Request a copy of your state criminal record and know where to find your federal and court records.
This lesson builds toward: Using your state's official website, you will request a copy of your own criminal record and find where to get federal and court records, writing down the form name, fee, fee waiver and nearest fingerprint site.
You cannot fix what you cannot see. Before you apply for any record relief, get a copy of your own record. It shows each arrest and case, the county, the dates and how each case ended. Records often have mistakes or missing outcomes.
In California, the Department of Justice (DOJ) runs a Record Review. If you live in California, you fill out form BCIA 8016RR, mark Record Review as the type of application, and take it to a Live Scan site to be fingerprinted. DOJ charges a $25 processing fee (a fee waiver is available), and the Live Scan site charges its own fee. If you live outside California, you mail form BCIA 8705 with a fingerprint card. Check oag.ca.gov for the current form and fee.
Your record may live in more than one place. A state record covers state cases. The FBI keeps a national record called an Identity History Summary; check fbi.gov for how to request it and the current fee. Each county court also keeps its own case files, which you can ask for at the clerk's office.
If you find a mistake on your California record, DOJ sends a form called BCIA 8706, the Claim of Alleged Inaccuracy or Incompleteness, with your record. You mail it back with proof.
Step by step:
- Choose which record you need first: usually your state record.
- In California, fill out BCIA 8016RR and mark Record Review.
- Get fingerprinted at a Live Scan site and pay the fees, or ask about the fee waiver.
- When the record arrives, list each case: county, case number if shown, date, charge and outcome.
- Mark anything that looks wrong or missing, and keep the record in a safe folder.
Words to know:
- Criminal record: the official list of your arrests and court cases kept by the state or the FBI.
- Live Scan: a machine that takes your fingerprints digitally and sends them to the state.
- Record Review: the California DOJ service that lets you see your own state record.
- Disposition: how a case ended, for example dismissed, convicted or acquitted.
Official sources:
- California DOJ: Record Review (request your own record)
- California DOJ: Apply for a fee waiver
- FBI: Identity History Summary checks
Try it now: Find the official page where your state lets you request your own record (in California, oag.ca.gov Record Review). Write down the form name, the fee, whether there is a fee waiver, and the nearest place to get fingerprinted.
You can now request a copy of your state record, say where your FBI and court records are kept, and spot mistakes to challenge.

check.q: In California, what do you need to do to see your own state record?
options: Fill out the DOJ Record Review form and get fingerprinted at a Live Scan site
Ask an AI assistant to look it up
check.why: California's DOJ Record Review uses a form and Live Scan fingerprints.

check.q: You get your record and see a case that is not yours. What would you do?
options: Challenge it with the official form for mistakes
check.why: Getting your record lets you catch mistakes and challenge them officially.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: What the record relief words mean
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the difference between expungement, dismissal, sealing, set-aside, a certificate of rehabilitation and a pardon.
This lesson builds toward: Given the record relief words, you will explain the difference between expungement, sealing, set-aside or dismissal, a certificate of rehabilitation and a pardon, with one plain, correct sentence for each.
People say expungement for almost any way of cleaning a record, but the real words and what they do are different in every state. Knowing the words helps you ask the right questions.
Expungement usually means the record is erased or destroyed. Sealing means the record still exists but most people, such as many employers and landlords, cannot see it. A set-aside or dismissal means the court reopens a conviction and dismisses it, so in most cases you no longer have to say you were convicted. California's courts say true expungement does not exist in California; what people call expungement there is usually a dismissal.
A certificate of rehabilitation is a court order saying you have lived a law-abiding life since your sentence. In some states it can help with licenses or be a step toward a pardon. A pardon is forgiveness from a governor (for state crimes) or the President (for federal crimes).
None of these always wipes a record clean for every purpose. Some government jobs, licenses, firearms rules and immigration still look at old cases. A lawyer can tell you what each option does for you.
Words to know:
- Expungement: erasing or destroying a record; in many places the word is used loosely for any record clean-up.
- Sealing: the record still exists but most of the public cannot see it.
- Set-aside or dismissal: a court reopens a conviction and dismisses it.
- Certificate of rehabilitation: a court order saying you have lived a law-abiding life since your sentence.
- Pardon: official forgiveness from a governor or the President.
Official sources:
- California Courts Self-Help Guide: Clean your record
Try it now: Make a small chart with five rows: expungement, sealing, set-aside or dismissal, certificate of rehabilitation, pardon. Next to each, write one plain sentence about what it does. Then write one question about your own case to ask a lawyer.
You can now explain the main kinds of record relief in plain words and say why you still ask a lawyer what each one does for you.

check.q: What does sealing a record usually do?
options: Keeps the record but hides it from most people
Turns a felony into a ticket
check.why: A sealed record still exists, but most people cannot see it.

check.q: You are not sure which relief fits your case. What would you do?
options: Pick the one with the nicest name
File for all of them at once
Write down your question and ask a lawyer or legal aid
Ask a friend who had a different case
check.why: A lawyer or legal aid can tell which relief fits your own case.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Federal, state and California Clean Slate
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Tell whether each of your cases is federal or state and check whether California's automatic relief may already apply.
This lesson builds toward: Given your list of cases, you will identify whether each case is federal or state and check whether automatic relief may apply, with every case labeled and a plan to check your newest record.
Each case belongs to the system that charged it. A state case went through a county court and is handled under that state's laws. A federal case went through a United States District Court. State relief cannot clear a federal conviction, and federal relief does not clear state convictions.
Relief for federal convictions is very limited. The main path is a presidential pardon. The US Department of Justice's Office of the Pardon Attorney takes pardon applications from people with federal convictions who have finished their sentence.
California has Clean Slate laws. Every month the California DOJ checks its records, marks eligible arrests and convictions as receiving relief, and tells the courts. You do not have to file anything for this automatic relief, and DOJ does not tell you when it happens. A 2022 law, SB 731, added many more felonies starting in 2024.
Automatic relief limits who can see a case, but it does not dismiss, seal or erase it. Some employers who use fingerprint checks, such as police and schools, may still see it. To know if you got it, request your own record. For dismissal, sealing or a reduced charge, you still file with the court.
Step by step:
- For each case on your record, write the court: a county court means state, a US District Court means federal.
- For federal cases, look at the Office of the Pardon Attorney's page.
- In California, check your new DOJ record for a note that relief was granted.
- List the cases that still need a court petition.
Words to know:
- Federal case: a case charged by the US government and heard in a US District Court.
- State case: a case charged under state law and heard in a county court.
- Clean Slate: laws that give some record relief automatically, without a petition.
- Petition: a written request you file asking a court to do something.
Official sources:
- California DOJ: Automatic record relief (Penal Code 851.93 and 1203.425)
- US DOJ Office of the Pardon Attorney: Apply for clemency
Try it now: Using your record or what you remember, list each case and write state or federal next to it. If you live in California, write down whether your newest DOJ record shows automatic relief for any case, or plan to request it to find out.
You can now sort your cases into federal and state, explain what California's automatic relief does and does not do, and list which cases still need a petition.

check.q: Your case was heard in a county superior court. What kind of case is it?
check.why: County superior courts hear state cases.

check.q: You live in California and think automatic relief may apply to an old case. What would you do?
options: Request your newest DOJ record and look for the relief note
check.why: Your newest DOJ record shows whether automatic relief was applied.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Get help, prepare and use your rights

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding free legal help
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find two free places that can help you with record relief and prepare for the first call.
This lesson builds toward: Using official and nonprofit sources, you will find two free places that help with record relief and prepare questions for the first call, with name, phone, hours and three questions for each, and no paid service that guarantees results.
Record relief laws are complicated, and a mistake can cost you months. The good news: a lot of help is free. California's court self-help guide has a Get started form that asks a few questions and gives instructions for your situation, plus a legal help page.
Places that often help for free include court self-help centers, legal aid offices, public defender offices (about 19 California counties have record-cleaning programs), law school clinics, reentry organizations, and one-day clean slate clinics. In California, the Clear My Record service connects people to legal help in some counties.
If you are not a US citizen, talk to an immigration lawyer before you file anything. Court actions can affect immigration status, and some relief does not count for immigration.
Be careful of anyone who promises to erase your record for a big fee, guarantees a result, or asks for payment before telling you what they will do. Real help explains your options first.
Step by step:
- Go to your state court's self-help website (in California, selfhelp.courts.ca.gov, Clean your record).
- Find two free helpers: a self-help center, legal aid, public defender program or clean slate clinic.
- Write down their phone number, hours and what they ask you to bring.
- Prepare three questions before you call.
- If you are not a citizen, contact an immigration lawyer first.
Words to know:
- Legal aid: free legal help for people with low incomes.
- Public defender: a government lawyer for people who cannot pay; many also run record-clearing programs.
- Clean slate clinic: an event where volunteer lawyers help people fill out record relief papers, usually for free.
Official sources:
- California Courts Self-Help Guide: Clean your record
- California Courts Self-Help Guide: Legal help to clean your record
Try it now: Find two free legal helpers near you for record relief. For each, write the name, phone number, hours and what to bring. Then write three questions you will ask, such as: Which of my cases can be cleared? Which kind of relief fits? How long will it take?
You can now find free legal help for record relief, prepare for the first call and spot paid offers that are warning signs.

check.q: Which is a free place to look for record relief help?
options: A website that guarantees results for a big fee
check.why: Court self-help centers offer free help with court forms.

check.q: Someone promises to clear your record for sure if you pay $1,000 today. What would you do?
options: Walk away and contact free legal help instead
Give them your case details to check
check.why: Guarantees and big up-front fees are warning signs.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Preparing and filing with help
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a record-relief folder that a lawyer or clinic can use to file for you.
This lesson builds toward: Given your cases and proof of your life now, you will build a record-relief folder a lawyer or clinic can use, with each case's county, year and charge and a checklist of proof still needed.
Lawyers and clinics can help you much faster when you arrive organized. Build one folder, paper or digital, with everything about your cases.
Put in: a copy of your record; a list of each case with the county, case number, year and charge; proof you finished probation, parole or programs; proof of paid fines, fees and restitution, or what is still owed; and proof of your life now, such as job letters, certificates, classes, treatment, volunteer work and letters of support.
Your helper will choose the right forms, file them with the right court and tell you whether there is a hearing. Ask them to explain each form before you sign. Keep copies of everything you file and write down every date.
After the court grants relief, ask for a copy of the order. A few months later, request your record again to make sure it was updated. If it was not, contact your helper or the court clerk.
Step by step:
- Start one folder for your record relief.
- Add your record and a list of each case: county, case number, year, charge.
- Add proof of finished probation, parole and programs, and of fines paid or owed.
- Add proof of your life now: work, school, treatment, volunteering, support letters.
- Take the folder to your helper; keep copies of everything filed and all dates.
- After relief is granted, keep the order and check your record again later.
Words to know:
- Case number: the number a court gives each case; it helps find the file fast.
- Restitution: money a court orders you to pay to the victim of a crime.
- Hearing: a meeting in court where a judge listens and decides.
- Order: the judge's written decision.
Try it now: Start your record-relief folder today. Write the list of cases you know about (county, year, charge) and a checklist of the proof you still need to collect. Put a star next to the first two papers you will get this week.
You can now build a record-relief folder, work with a helper to file, and check afterward that your record was updated.

options: The number a court gives each case
check.why: Each court case has its own case number.

check.q: The court granted your relief. What would you do later?
options: Request your record again to make sure it was updated
Tell employers you have no record without checking
check.why: Checking your record again makes sure the relief shows up.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Fair-chance hiring and your rights
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain California's Fair Chance Act and prepare a short rehabilitation statement for an employer.
This lesson builds toward: Using California's Fair Chance Act, you will explain when an employer can check your record and write a short rehabilitation statement, with a statement that is honest, short and says what you have done since.
California's Fair Chance Act covers public employers and private employers with five or more employees, with some exceptions such as jobs where a law requires a background check. Most covered employers cannot ask about your conviction history on an application, run a background check, or post ads saying No Felons, before they offer you a job.
After a conditional job offer, they may run a check, but they can never use arrests that did not lead to a conviction (with limited exceptions), convictions that were sealed, dismissed or expunged, cases cleared after diversion, or, in most cases, convictions more than seven years old. They cannot reject you just for having a record. They must look at your situation and the job.
If they want to take back the offer, they must tell you in writing, give you a copy of the report and list the convictions, and give you at least five business days to respond with evidence of rehabilitation, or to show a mistake on the report. If you think an employer broke the law, you can contact the California Civil Rights Department. Other states and cities have their own rules, often called ban the box; check yours.
Prepare a short, honest statement now: what happened in one sentence, what you have done since, and why you are ready for this job. Gather proof, such as certificates, finished programs, support letters and a bonding letter if you have one.
Step by step:
- Check whether your state or city has a fair-chance or ban-the-box law.
- Write one sentence about what happened, without excuses.
- Write two or three sentences about what you have done since.
- End with why you are ready for this job.
- Gather proof and keep it with your statement.
Words to know:
- Fair Chance Act: California's law limiting when and how employers can look at conviction history.
- Conditional job offer: a job offer that depends on something, such as a background check.
- Ban the box: laws that remove the criminal record question from job applications.
- Evidence of rehabilitation: proof of how your life has changed, such as programs finished and support letters.
Official sources:
- California Civil Rights Department: Fair Chance Act
- California Civil Rights Department: Criminal History and Employment fact sheet (June 2025)
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page record-relief action plan. Include where you will get your record, each case and the relief that might fit it, the free legal help you will contact first, the papers you will gather, and your short rehabilitation statement for employers.
You can now explain your fair-chance hiring rights in California, find out the rules in your state, and answer an employer about your record with a short, honest statement and proof.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Getting the record No plan, or plans to use a private background-check site. Names the official place to request the record and the fingerprint site. Also notes the fee, fee waiver and where to get a federal record if needed. Cases and possible relief Cases are missing, or none is labeled state or federal. Each known case has county, year, charge, state or federal, and a possible kind of relief. Notes which cases to check for automatic relief and one question for a lawyer. Free legal help No helper named, or a paid service that guarantees results. A free legal helper to contact first, with phone and hours. A second helper and three questions to ask are also written down. Papers to gather No list of papers. A checklist of records and proof of life now to gather. The first two papers to get this week are starred. Rehabilitation statement Missing, too long, or not honest. A short, honest statement: what happened in a sentence, what you have done since, and why you are ready. Practiced out loud and mentions proof like certificates or letters of support. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Under California's Fair Chance Act, when can most covered employers run a background check?
check.why: Covered employers wait until after a conditional offer to check your record.

check.q: An employer asks about your past after making you an offer. What would you do?
options: Give a short, honest statement about what you have done since
Tell a long story about the case
Refuse to say anything and leave
check.why: A short, honest rehabilitation statement shows you are ready for the job.
